newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close lower in Greenspan aftermath.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close lower in Greenspan aftermath.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower on Thursday after stronger-than-expected durable goods data did little to allay fears of tighter monetary policy.

Volume was strong but prices traded in relatively narrow bands compared to the massive selloff on Wednesday, after Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan warned the Fed could tighten without strong inflation numbers, and said the soaring stock market could be based on overexuberance.
The 30-year bond closed 12/32 lower at 97-23/32 to yield 6.80 percent.

Bond prices opened lower and sank further after data showed durable goods orders up 3.6 percent versus expectations of a 1.5 percent rise. In midafternoon, factors including another strong inflation indicator and sales sparked by techicals pressured prices as much as 3/4-point lower.

"It's a very dispirited market right now," said Anthony Karadakis, senior financial economist at First National Bank of Chicago. He noted that "The market was deeply disturbed yesterday on Greenspan and had been disturbed days before ... Then we get another surprisingly strong economic number in durable goods this morning and we have nowhere to go but down."

The Economic Cycle Research Institute said its weekly inflation gauge rose to 108.3. In addition, hedge funds were said to be large sellers of five-year paper and heavy central bank selling was rumored in two-year notes.

Also circulating was a Johnson Smick International report saying Greenspan had been backed into a corner with Wednesday's comments and would be forced to tighten by 25 basis points should the stock market ignore his warnings.
However, Karadakis dismissed the notion that Johnson Smick was influential enough to drive the market. "We were going down and it was obvious," he said.

"People feel we had two lousy auctions this week and Greenspan's comments definitely had a more threatening tone than previously," Karadakis said. "The bias right now is lower," he said, predicting the 30-year bond yield would edge back to around 7.0 percent until significant evidence suggested the economy was slowing.

"I see a market coming to grips with the fact that the risks for inflation and tightening are all on the upside," said John Williams, chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust Co. "Over the past couple of days this has finally made its way into the price of assets."

Williams said the economy continued to run above its noninflationary speed limit and the temporary factors Greenspan mentioned in his testimony were just about worked through, including rising worker anxiety levels and the deceleration in the cost of benefits.
This would become manifest in the form of higher wages and higher consumer prices, he said.
"Before yesterday the financial markets seemed to be assuming we had attained nirvana -- that we would have no inflationary pressure and no recession for as long as we all lived," Williams said.

Trading volume was again very heavy after Wednesday saw some $118.7 billion change hands. About $105.7 billion had been traded by about 1600 EST/2100 GMT, marking the first time since last February that volume exceeded $100 billion on two consecutive days, said GovPX senior analyst Maureen Mooney.
She said the session's late number was 27 percent above an average Thursday in the first quarter of 1996.
Treasury's auction of $23 billion of 45-day cash management bills came in at an average rate of 5.16 percent and the average on the $19.25 billion one-year bills was 5.36 percent.
Three-month bill rates rose two basis points to 5.07 percent. Six-month bill rates were five basis points higher at 5.14 percent and year-bill rates were two basis points higher 5.33 percent.

Two-year notes ended down 2/32 at 99-20/32, yielding 6.08 percent. Five-year notes closed at 99-15/32, down 5/32, yielding 6.38 percent. Ten-year notes ended at 98-25/32, down 7/32 to yield 6.56 percent.
